articles.title: Launch HN: Respan (YC W24) – Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins
articles.summary:
Hey HN, this is Andy from Respan (https://www.respan.ai). We are building an open-source Rust AI gateway. It is a decoupled gateway, so everything is a plugin, including different providers, protocols (MCP, voice), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features (fallbacks, PII redaction, smart routing).
Instead of packaging tons of providers and features into one gateway, Respan provides a small core and public interfaces that teams can use to assemble the AI infrastructure their application needs. That way, users can build their own features as additional plugins without having to change the gateway's core.
Here’s a video demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVv2ibXiTXM
There are countless LLM gateways and most of them solve a common problem: calling different providers from a single endpoint. However, adding new features can become prohibitively difficult. So developers can end up building another gateway to solve a specific problem.
We've been building our gateway based on LiteLLM since 2024, and now it's providing services for thousands of orgs. Each org needs different API key settings, routes, and limits. To support that, we kept wrapping LiteLLM, adding more features to it, and at one stage, our wrapper code exceeded 100,000 lines.
This January, a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection errors, and we had to roll back. We still haven't figured out the cause, but since then, we no longer upgrade LiteLLM directly and instead manually backport upstream fixes. These experiences made us realize that continuing to patch LiteLLM is not a sustainable long-term solution, and we had to redesign the gateway ourselves.
While redesigning our gateway, we wanted to make it easier to add features without breaking existing ones. Inspired by Nginx, we think an AI gateway should have a really small core, only responsible for dispatching events.
We believe that everything should be a plugin in our gateway, including providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), protocols (chat, realtime voice, MCP), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features for reliability and security (smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction through example plugins). Beyond that, we want developers to be able to easily extend the gateway's capabilities by adding their own plugins, without touching the core. Adding a provider, even your own, is dead simple, because quirks are plugins too and there’s nothing magical about them. A provider is a short file, Mistral’s is 22 lines, and each quirk, like Groq putting token usage in its own field, gets its own test.
Respan Gateway does more than let you call Claude or Gemini models from the OpenAI SDK. It handles tools, images, and reasoning protocols automatically: an application based on the OpenAI Realtime API can also use Gemini Live through the gateway, though not every feature translates. A simple chat app can use MCP tools configured in the gateway, without implementing MCP itself.
We also parse requests into a shared structure. When the client and provider use the same API, we preserve provider-specific fields in their native format, even if our shared structure doesn't have a field for them. That way, the gateway can write them back instead of dropping them.
Here’s how it works:
An adapter hands each HTTP or WebSocket connection to the first client format that recognizes it. The format exposes the request as a two-way stream of typed input and output events. The core runs plugins in registration order, allowing them to choose a provider, filter or wrap either stream, make additional calls, return a response, or refuse the request. A provider format then opens the upstream connection.
If the client and provider use the same format and no plugin changes the payload, the original bytes and protocol-specific fields can pass through unchanged. When formats differ, they translate through shared types for messages, tool calls, results, streams, and usage. This stream model can represent both one-shot HTTP requests and long-lived bidirectional sessions.
The gateway is open source at https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway under the MIT or Apache-2.0 license. You don't need to use Respan's hosted platform and can run it directly on your local machine. Build it from source, add your provider keys, and swap the base URL in a supported client. You can keep using the API your client already speaks. It's still pre-alpha.
We make money from our hosted platform (https://www.respan.ai/pricing), which runs the gateway for you with native observability and evals, along with unified billing.
If you’re building routing, tools, filtering, observability, or security for agents, we'd love to see it as a plugin. PLUGINS.md in the repo explains how to write one and links to the plugins we’ve created so far. Turning that into an ecosystem is basically our roadmap, and we welcome you to contribute your own plugins. We'd love to answer any questions and hear your feedback!

articles.title: NixOS Is Making Me Less Afraid
articles.summary:
Something funny happened a little while ago: I read about FreshRSS, and it
sounded nice, so I installed it on a server and started using it. That would
not have happened a year ago, but then again, a year ago I didn’t have any NixOS
servers.





For the past few years, my RSS feeds have lived locally on my phone only.
There was a good idea behind that, but it never quite worked in practice. For one,
many things are easier to read on a larger screen. But it was also brittle to
trust a phone app to manage the read/unread status of thousands of articles
across a hundred feeds. What I really wanted was a server-side feed aggregator. This is software
that runs on a server, manages RSS feeds, and then I can read the RSS feeds
either through a web interface, or through client applications. I’ve wanted that
for a while, but I’ve never taken the step, because it would be yet another side
project to maintain the deployment of.





But now, with some NixOS experience, adding a working FreshRSS configuration
(including backups) took 9 lines of Nix code. That installation has
just hands-off worked for the past few months. If or when that server breaks, I
can spin up a new one running the exact same configuration, probably in
something like 15 minutes. When we can do something like that, there is
literally no reason to not just try the new software.

articles.title: Pluralistic: The death of history's most successful publisher (20 Oct 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links The death of history's most successful publisher: Google has a scorching case of "main character syndrome." Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Civil War x 4,400 ceramic cats; Okaysellers; Frankenstein hat; Clockwork Fagin; Tracking trackers; "Fever Beach." Upcoming appearances: Victoria, Vancouver, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Couretnay, Vancouver, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. The death of history's most successful publisher (permalink) I published my first story in 1988, when I was 17 years old. Today, at 55, I've published more than 30 books, with three more coming in the next year or so. In the intervening years, I've spent a lot of time thinking and talking about publishing. I've had plenty of opportunity to reflect on publishing: I've been a bookseller and worked in libraries, I wrote a column for Publishers Weekly, self-published a few books of my own, published the first-ever book licensed under Creative Commons, and broke several Kickstarter records for audiobook projects. But most of all, I've worked with publishing professionals: publicists, marketing directors, operations people, copyeditors, and, above all, editors. My first novel editor was the magnificent Patrick Nielsen Hayden, who supported my publishing career from the very start, donating to help send me to the Clarion science fiction writers' workshop and inviting me to come read slush at Tor Books whenever I was in New York. Patrick didn't teach me everything I know about publishing, but he sure taught me a lot about publishing, and hardly a day goes by without my having cause to reflect on one of our many discussions over our decades-long professional and personal association. Out of all the things I learned about publishing from Patrick, one truth stands out above all: publishing is "the act of making something public." Publishing may or may not involve editing, layout, printing, binding, marketing or other activities that we associate with publishing houses, but publishing always involves identifying a work, identifying an audience, and finding ways to connect that work to that audience. This definition does a lot of useful work. For one thing, it locates publishing as part of the hard problem of human society, namely, "getting people to care about something that matters to you." Beyond publishing, this is the crux of politics, religion and commerce: https://pluralistic.net/2021/07/04/self-publishing/ For another, this definition lets us understand that (for most of its existence) Google was the most successful publisher in human history. No other institution of any kind connected more works with more audiences. Lots of people have heard of Google's wildly unsuccessful motto "Don't be evil," but far fewer are familiar with Google's wildly successful mission statement, "organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful." But all of that is in the past tense. With its AI projects – AI summaries, the Gemini chatbot – Google has abandoned the practice of "connecting works with audiences." Today, Google's function is to plunder all the works on the internet and chop them up and arrange them in an unimaginably vast, multidimensional array for the explicit purpose of preventing audiences from connecting with those works. For most of its history, Google operated in a virtuous cycle with publishers whereby they allowed Google to crawl their sites and Google located audiences and connected them with the pages on those sites. Today, that cycle has turned vicious, with Google acting as a parasite that extracts value from the web's publishers and offers nothing in return. This is entirely in keeping with the enshittification hypothesis: that once a platform is liberated from the disciplining forces of competition, regulation, labor and interoperability, it will squeeze its suppliers and users and harvest all the value for itself: https://pluralistic.net/2023/01/21/potemkin-ai/#hey-guys But AI represents a new phase in enshittification. Google has assayed enshittificatory gambits in the past, like deliberately worsening its search results in order to force you to search repeatedly, which gave the company more chances to show you ads: https://pluralistic.net/2024/04/24/naming-names/#prabhakar-raghavan But as sleazy as those gambits were, they were profitable. In some important sense, they were sustainable. Assuming Google could carry on indefinitely scamming its users in this way, they'd continue to bring in more cash than they spent, and continue to be the world's most successful publisher, connecting works and audiences (albeit in a deliberately degraded way). Contrast this with AI, the money-losingest endeavor in the history of human civilization. Google is losing hundreds of billions of dollars on AI. The more AI Google does, the worse the company's financial footing becomes. If Google does this for long enough, it may cease to exist altogether. This collapse can only be prolonged by Google's ongoing extraction of value from web publishers, who no longer have their works connected with audiences via Google search results. Instead, Google usurps those audiences, shows them as many ads as it can, and still loses money in the bargain. In Tim Wu's Age of Extraction, Wu lays out a thesis about how intermediaries – middlemen who perform a useful function connecting different groups, firms and individuals – are prone to developing "main character syndrome," abandoning their role as facilitators for others and abusing their position to make themselves the prime beneficiary of the transactions they facilitate: https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/691177/the-age-of-extraction-by-tim-wu/ Google has a scorching case of main character syndrome, and nowhere is that more obvious than in its AI-fueled transformation into web-scale parasite. The fact that this gambit might well destroy Google and the publishers the company once served – rather than merely enshittifying search with worse results and more ads – makes the whole thing look more like a Mafia bust-out than the enshittification of the first half of the 2020s: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bust_Out It's certainly an ignominious end for history's most successful publisher (as was). Observations:
There were way more people who successfully got October ship dates than I expected. It’s very close to even with November ship dates.


The fact that there are fewer December ship dates than January, is to me, a sign of Apple’s appreciation for the holidays. I think Apple is only promising “December” for shipments they are 100 percent certain they can deliver by Christmas. I bet a bunch of the orders promised for January will in fact ship in December — albeit perhaps too-late-for-Christmas December.


Apparently some configurations are getting an estimated date of February 1. I wish I’d listed February as an option, but I don’t think it would have made a big difference.


Per MacRumors today, some pre-order estimates are already moving up, like from early December to late November.



No one should mistake my audience as representative of the general public in any poll, but I bet my audience is at least ballpark representative of the general public when it comes to something like pre-ordering, at the crack of dawn, a new iPhone form factor that costs $2000 to $3200.
I didn’t ask on Bluesky because — despite launching over three years ago — it still lacks a poll feature. There’s some kind of third-party thing called poll.blue, but I couldn’t be bothered. ↩︎

articles.title: Death & Domains
articles.summary:
A recent piece on “forever domains” sparked bigger questions about permanence online: when domain owners die out, do we need new systems that don't rely on domains at all?

Should domains last forever? That’s not a new question for me, but it’s one that I’ve been thinking more about lately, especially since I ended up writing a story recently that posed this exact question.
Over at the new publication GraveSite, which covers the concept of death and grief with a reporter’s eye, I posed a question I’ve thought a lot about over the years: How can you keep a person’s digital identity alive even if their physical identity is long gone? For corporate entities this is actually reasonably easy—succession plans and all that, ensuring someone is paying the bills long-term.
But people aren‘t corporations, and business structures like domain registrars and web hosts often treat us as consumers. Which means that when we aren’t around to consume, and to pay money in exchange for that consumption, we’re going to be the first to lose our digital plot in the ground. There’s no internet cemetery, and we have a relatively limited number of archives that can hold our digital histories.
Which means that, when we go offline, so will our digital identities, eventually. It’ll take longer, but that credit card isn’t going to pay for itself. If you’re a writer or creative, this is a real risk, and the answers for solving this simply aren’t very good.
My piece goes over some of the novel solutions out there, including a nonprofit initiative to essentially take ownership of websites and pay the bills in your absence.
I’m happy with the piece, but don’t want to spoil it, so I’ll simply encourage you to read. But I wanted to spend a second thinking about a the second-order effects of this: If domains last forever, at what point do we need to start over?


You might save a loved one’s artifacts in a box like this (or maybe even a nicer one). Should you have a similar kind of package for their digital data? (Jernej Breznik/Unsplash)
This was an argument I heard from a couple of readers about this topic. There’s a finite number of domains—at what point are the domains already here going to crowd out people that left a long time ago. I own the domain erniesmith.net that I use to promote my freelance work; if I decided to sell it to a service that aims to keep a domain around “forever,” am I screwing over later generations of Ernie Smiths?
It’s hard to say, but I do think it speaks to a longer-term architecture problem that the internet will eventually face, a crossroads as our domain owners die out, the domain maybe not being relevant anymore but their websites certainly having some value. And maybe the solution to this problem is to create new systems for distributing information online that don’t necessarily rely on domains.
One commenter on my post, Alex Russell (a former Google Chrome engineer now working on Microsoft Edge), pointed to the idea of Web Packages, a concept where websites could be distributed in full without the need for any attached domain or even expected online access.
It was an idea that originated with the Chrome team, but found little to no uptake with other browser-makers, eventually falling into the abyss of Web standards obscurities. (The project currently lives with the Web Incubator Community Group (WICG).) It arguably deserves to be revisited as the problem of dead websites and dead owners becomes a bigger problem. For one thing, it helps to resolve some of the bigger, more annoying problems with old websites—that they’re often required to be static when they’ve fallen into disuse, that they often don’t support https like modern sites do, and that they can carry latent security issues, much like how an old book can grow dust and mold if not managed properly. (In fact, one of the listed uses for web packages is to create an easy-to-distribute format for researching security exploits.)
Should the domain system itself be seen as temporary? Should we treat old websites more like books whose volumes can be picked up at will when all is said and done? That’s a provocative idea, and one that I think deserves more discussion in the current climate.
But one thing I’ll say is that our system is completely upside down if your website stands a better chance of being around in 100 years if it’s a Facebook profile or a forgotten Blogger or LiveJournal site than if you put in the work to carefully put it on the internet yourself.
Anyway, I look forward to talking about these issues with the GraveSite team on October 27, when I’ll be taking part in their HellFireside Chat on digital death. If this topic at all appeals to you, hope to see you there.

Domain-Free Links
As the Mullenweg turns: Get ready for some drama, folks. Fortune has a feature explaining what, exactly, happened with Matt Mullenweg last month when he very briefly was booted from his CEO role with Automattic. As you might guess, it has to do with the ongoing WP Engine mess.

A quick shout-out to friend of Tedium Sean Malseed, a.k.a. Action Retro, who publicly discussed his health issues with his audience. That stuff isn’t fun, and he’s not all the way through it, but I’m glad he’s still with us. After all, someone needs to put Haiku on a toaster, and I’d prefer if he did it.
Tying to my prior discussion of ArtCraft, I think that the rising trend of reverse engineering of technology you already own is a good thing, especially when it counters ugly corporate practices. Smart TVs, as highlighted by 404 Media, are an excellent starting point here.
--
Thanks to the team at GraveSite for letting me write about this important issue. (You should definitely subscribe if the topic of death is one that you find interesting.) Wanna share this piece? Here’s a quick link.
By the way, we just gave the Tedium Shopping Network an infusion of fresh products. Curious? Give it a look.

articles.title: From the DF Archive: Should a CEO Be a Nerd About Their Company’s Products?
articles.summary:
Back in 2022, I quoted from an interesting post by Ben Schlappig at One Mile at a Time, where he wrote:
I’ve had the opportunity to interact with quite a few senior
airline executives over the years, and I find that their knowledge
about competitors is typically one extreme or the other:
Some airline executives literally couldn’t tell you the first
thing about their competitors, and have no knowledge of their
passenger experience, fleet, etc.
Some airline executives know literally everything about their
competitors, down to being able to tell you how many seats
competitors have on specific planes
I find there are very few executives who are just kind of in the
middle, as it’s pretty polarizing. Either they know virtually
everything about competitors, or nearly nothing. Without naming
any names, I’ll say that generally speaking there’s a high
correlation between airlines that have a great passenger
experience, and airlines that have executives that keep very close
tabs on the competition.
And I wrote:
If the CEO’s primary perspective on the company is via
spreadsheets — if it’s all just P&L to them — that company is
not going to excel at quality. Or if they do excel at quality,
they won’t for long.
I think Tim Cook was truly an exception in this regard. He’s not a product guy, and never pretended to be. He is a spreadsheet guy. But he clearly realized that about himself, and he understood that Apple’s entire point is delivering great products and experiences. But I think Ternus is a breath of fresh air in this regard. Apple didn’t immediately switch to decision-making by quantifiable numbers under Cook, but incrementally, year-by-year, decision-making by quantifiable numbers took over.
You simply cannot assign numeric values to everything, and some of those things that cannot be quantified are the most important things. Apple needs a CEO who makes some major product decisions by gut alone.
 ★

articles.title: How to install an app on your Commodore 64
articles.summary:
It’s time to install an app! But here in 1986, we still call them “programs,” not apps. So, you’ll want to set aside some time to get started installing a program.
Since you have a Commodore 64, there are really only two options for getting new programs this month: COMPUTE!’s Gazette and RUN, and you have to hope that one of those magazines isn’t sold out at the book store. So let’s get going.
Go To The App Book Store
You will need to ask your mom if you can ride your bike to the mall. The dirt mall is closer, but the magazine stand at the dirt mall doesn’t carry any computer magazines, so you’ll need to take a longer ride to the good mall, where the book store actually has computer magazines. It’s a couple of miles to the mall, so usually you would have a friend come with you, but you called their house and nobody picked up, so today it’s a solo trip.
Only one book store carries computer magazines at this mall; the other one only carries magazines about “serious” topics, but they can order back issues of a magazine for you if you want, you just have to wait a few weeks and they’ll call you when it comes in.
The guy at the book store doesn’t know the difference between the different computer magazines, so you can’t ask him if they have the one you want in stock, and he’s probably not going to answer a kid anyway. So you just have to go through all the titles one by one, and hope nobody put a copy of People or Omni in front of it by accident.
There are no ratings, and no reviews of the programs themselves. The closest thing you get is the magazine’s own reviews of hardware — modems, mostly — and a cover that promises you the issue has the thing you want. This month’s cover has a “Buyer’s Guide To Modems” banner across the top.

Once you’ve got a copy of COMPUTE!’s Gazette and you’re checking out at the store, you can see that it’s three dollars for the magazine (about nine bucks in 2026 money). If you’re lucky enough to have a five dollar bill, you’ll still have two dollars left over after buying the magazine. That means you’ll have enough money to swing by the record store later and grab a 45 of one of the new singles, like Sheila E.’s “A Love Bizarre,” written by Prince, or The Bangles’ “Manic Monday,” written by Prince, or Prince and the Revolution’s “Kiss,” written by Prince.
Pick Your Program
Now it’s time to race home with the new magazine in hand. You’ll have to wait for everybody to get off of the TV that’s by the computer so you can switch it over to the channel the computer is on and get down to work.
Turn on the switch, and you’re at the blinking blue cursor where it says READY. while the screen is still warming up a bit.
When it comes to installing apps programs, it’s all about options, and this month, we’re spoiled: there are two! They’re both games: Survivor, an arena game where, “if you’re quick of mind, eye, and hand, you might outfox your opponent,” and Shifter. Truly, an embarrassment of riches. Since Survivor is the one on the cover, we’ll go with that one.
(Two or three programs a month is pretty typical. That’s… the app store.)
Type It In
Getting this program running is standard stuff — you just read the article on page 36 that describes the game, and then flip to pages 106 and 107 where there’s the code for a short BASIC loader, and then continue on to pages 107 and 108, where there are 345 rows of densely-packed listings consisting of 9 hexadecimal character pairs, all of which have to be typed in perfectly with zero errors or else your entire game will refuse to run.
A quick sample of the early part of your task looks like this:

After you’re done typing that page in, you’re about a quarter of the way done, assuming you didn’t make any mistakes.
Wait, what’s that? Where are you supposed to be typing these in? Simply type them into the MLX program where you… wait, what’s that? You don’t have the MLX utility that’s used to type in machine language code for games and programs listed in the magazine?
Oh, don’t worry, you’ll just need to type in the code for that program. There’s an article explaining what MLX is, which you can read really quickly on page 93, and then you’ll find the code for it on page 94. That one’s only 100 lines of code, so it should be easy enough to type in. And of course, you’ll know if you made any mistakes when typing, thanks to the Automatic Proofreader.
Wait, you don’t have the Automatic Proofreader program?
Well, no worries. It’s only another 31 lines of BASIC code, which you can find on page 97. (This one you have to type in perfectly on your own; there’s no proofreader for the proofreader.) Once you do that, you’re all set.

Now, you can just use the program that lets you enter the program to make your program. It should only take about half an hour to type in the code for the Automatic Proofreader, and maybe another hour or two for MLX. Let’s call it two hours total between them.
After that, Survivor is ~30 lines of BASIC plus ~350 lines of hex code, so… maybe six hours? But at least MLX will catch any typos as you go.
Once all of this is complete, be sure to save your work to a floppy disk so you don’t have to type it all in again! If all you have is a cassette deck and you’re saving to tape, it’s going to take probably 10–20 minutes of staring at a blank screen when you save, so set aside some time for that.
In total, it should only take you about 8 hours to have Survivor ready to play, plus however long it takes you to get to the mall, buy a magazine, and come back.
Ready To Play
(Click or tap to get started.)

[This is Survivor by Kevin Mykytyn and Mark Tuttle, from COMPUTE!’s Gazette, March 1986, running in the VICE emulator. The game loads and runs on its own, which takes a few seconds.]
Controls: the yellow player uses W/A/S/D to move and F to fire; the cyan player uses the arrow keys to move and Enter to fire.
Next Steps
The Download
Someday, rather than typing all of this in, you might be able to use your 300 baud modem to download already-created versions of these games and tools. You could dial a local BBS, if there’s one nearby. If you’re unlucky, the only one you can reach is a long-distance call, and you’ll be paying by the minute for as long as you’re connected. Or you could look for a local dial-up number for the Quantum Link online service (which will eventually evolve into America Online!).
Transfer times can range from tens of minutes to hours, and of course during those calls, you are tying up what’s usually the sole voice phone line for the household. Anyone picking up a phone handset in the house threatens to knock your connection offline, forcing you to start the whole process all over again.
Customization
Now that you’ve enjoyed your game of Survivor, there are some fun ways to customize your little computer and give it a personal touch.
Just for context, here’s a to-scale comparison of the screen resolution of your Commodore 64 to the dimensions of an iPhone Duo’s unfolded screen.
Commodore 64 screen compared to the iPhone Duo inner display, at the same pixel scale
A 2670 by 1878 pixel rectangle represents the iPhone Duo inner display. In its top-left corner, drawn at true size, is the Commodore 64 screen: 384 by 272 pixels including border, with a 320 by 200 pixel text area. The C64 fits about 48 times into the Duo display. On hover or focus, the C64 shows its READY. prompt and the Duo shows the 180 by 180 pixel App Store icon at the same scale.

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { .c64cmp { --phone: #2c2c2e; --ink: #f5f5f7; --rule: #a1a1a6; } }
.c64cmp .phone { fill: var(--phone); }

.c64cmp .sub { fill: var(--rule); font: 400 44px/1.2 -apple-system, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif; }

.c64cmp:hover .reveal, .c64cmp:focus .reveal { opacity: 1; }

Commodore 64

Icon for scale

Hover over (or tap) the comparison to see a C64 prompt and an App Store icon at the same scale.

You can’t change the wallpaper on your Commodore 64, but you can easily change the background colors for both the center area of the screen and the border. All you have to do is manually assign the proper numeric color code to the correct memory register corresponding to the values of each of those settings.
Memory address 53281 will set the background color for the primary content area, and a color code of 1 sets a nice readable white background, so it only takes a simple POKE 53281,1 command at the prompt, and you’re all set. Similarly, POKE 53280,4 will make the border of the screen a nice bright purple color, and of course there are a full complement of 16 colors to choose from.
Naturally, none of this customization is stored anywhere permanent, and it will all be lost if you turn off your computer or run a program.
READY.
I hope you’ve enjoyed this brief overview of how to get one game running on your Commodore 64, and perhaps gained a little appreciation for how things have gotten a bit simpler over the years.
Also, I will be entertaining a motion to return to calling our software “programs” instead of apps once more. Perhaps we could use the term to distinguish the software that’s created by humans actually typing things in, as opposed to the kind that’s merely generated by machines?

articles.title: Barack Obama on the Trump Administration’s Intimidation Campaign Against Congresswoman Ilhan Omar
articles.summary:
Barack Obama, in a 430-word essay:
It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government
can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their
political beliefs or what they say. But that’s exactly what the
Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of
Minnesota. [...]
The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to
engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should
outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about
Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the
new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.
Thoughtful, sharp, and eloquent as ever.
But Obama posted this essay on X, which, I have been told in the past week, shows that he in fact is a Nazi sympathizer, a fascist, a pedophile, and unconcerned about racism. As surprised as I was to learn those things about myself, I’m equally surprised to learn them about President Obama, whom I heretofore considered a thoughtful statesman and moral compass.
Either that, or, Threads, Bluesky, and Mastodon have relegated themselves into irrelevance by allowing their discourse to be dominated by a fringe of unhinged kooks who want to be angry and want everyone else to be angry.
 ★
